planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past last frost; this 1922 AAS-winning bush snap bean tolerates heat better than many modern bush types, so successive sowings through midsummer keep pods coming.

directions: Sow seed directly into warm soil after frost danger passes, spacing plants to allow good air movement around the dense bushy canopy. Pods set heavily even in hot, humid weather, carrying slight purple flecking on a medium-dark green round pod. Pick every two to three days once pods reach five to six inches to keep them snapping tender and to encourage continued flowering. Avoid working around wet plants to reduce the spread of bacterial and fungal leaf diseases common to bush beans.

planting.note: Wait until soil is reliably warm before direct sowing, since this long-season dry bean needs a full frost-free window to fill and dry down properly on the bush.

directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost risk has passed, growing this classic sturdy bush bean through summer to its full dry-bean maturity. Leave pods on the plant until they rattle and the foliage yellows and dries, since this variety is grown for its dense, deep-maroon dry seed rather than for snap eating. Pull whole plants or cut at the base once most pods are crisp and brown, then finish drying under cover before shelling and storing the beans. This is the familiar deep-colored kidney bean of chili, bean salads, and red beans and rice.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed; this widely adapted bush type sets a reliable crop even in cooler, wetter summers that can trouble other dry beans.

directions: Sow directly outdoors once frost has passed and soil temperatures are consistently warm, growing on a sturdy, medium-sized bush that adapts well across a wide range of climates. Allow pods to mature fully on the plant until they turn tan and papery and rattle with dry seed inside, which distinguishes this variety grown for drying rather than for fresh snap pods. Harvest by pulling or cutting whole plants once most pods are dry, then cure them further indoors before threshing. The thin-skinned, silky-textured beans hold their shape well in soups, salads, and baked bean dishes.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 55°F; vigorous foliage on this hybrid helps shade developing fruit from sunscald.

directions: Start seed indoors under warm conditions and transplant seedlings out after all frost danger has passed, giving plants room to build the heavy foliage cover that protects fruit from sun scorch. Fruit sets as extra-large, thick-walled blocky bells that can be harvested green or left on the plant to sweeten and ripen fully to red. This disease-resistant hybrid holds up well against bacterial leaf spot and other common pepper pressures, making it a dependable choice for stuffing peppers or thick slicing. Pick regularly with pruners to avoid snapping brittle branches and to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season.
